title: Former ARPA-H director Renee Wegrzyn wants to solve science’s ‘magic hands’ problem
description:
Renee Wegrzyn spent her career building the future of American science—including the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, or ARPA-H, the White House agency created to accelerate health breakthroughs.

Then the Trump administration showed her the door. Wegrzyn cofounded Transfyr to tackle what she calls one of the most overlooked issues in science: the magic hands problem. She explains why fixing this unglamorous bottleneck is the prerequisite for everything AI promises to deliver in medicine, and why she can feel the next Sputnik moment coming—even if she can’t quite name it yet.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by Robert Safian, former editor-in-chief of Fast Company. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

You were at ARPA-H, the inaugural director of a White House effort to accelerate health research. You were amped up about the possibilities, but with the Trump administration, you had to pivot. Was it hard not to take it personally that they wanted different leadership?

I’ll tell you, I’m still amped up about it. It’s still an amazing idea. Obviously, DARPA [the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency] has been around for almost 80 years. I hope ARPA-H will have the same longevity and continue to live on today.

I’m a builder. I love to take things forward and really show what’s possible. So was it hard when I left? Of course it was hard. I had a really unusual appointment: I was a presidential appointee, but I was term-limited, so I served through the transition and had a few weeks in the new administration. I served in “Trump one,” by the way, as well.

So it was a great opportunity to make sure they really understood why we built the agency. We needed an ARPA-H because there was something missing in the way we were doing science broadly, which was: How do you move really quickly? How do you get focused on a problem versus building a general knowledge set? I was able to show them what we were building and convince them that it was worth keeping around. I couldn’t be more proud of the agency and its perseverance.

So your new business, Transfyr—The New York Times wrote about you, and the article kept referring to “magic hands.” I’m curious what magic hands are. What problem is Transfyr trying to solve or address?

You probably have your favorite dish, or your parents’ or grandparents’ favorite dish. Sometimes they just have the magic hands. Nobody can cook it like they do. Nobody can make it taste the special way they can. And that happens in science as well. There are some scientists who just have the knack and can deliver really great science over and over.

The challenge is that a lot of those scientists are such experts they can hardly describe what they’re doing. It’s an art in some ways. And so the magic hands idea was really a testament to what those scientists can do in the lab.

The pipeline we’re creating at Transfyr is: Can we create computer vision and perception tools to capture the work of science as it’s being done so that we understand, if the protocol says, “Mix the cells,” whether someone is inverting the tube in a certain gentle way, while another researcher may be rigorously shaking or vortexing it, which could destroy the sample?

Those little things, compounded over the many decisions a scientist may make over the course of several hours of experimentation, lead to what is called magic hands.

Was this an issue you saw at ARPA-H, the sort of breakthroughs that were trapped in a single lab in some ways?

Where that manifested at DARPA and at ARPA-H was in a realization, through my career, of how fragile breakthroughs are. Usually, the way a breakthrough is first communicated to the world is through a research publication, a Science or Nature paper. That paper is not a product. It’s not commercializable. It’s not ready for a patient that day. That’s the starting gun for what is going to happen.

The ARPAs of this world are really fantastic at getting to that initial breakthrough and demonstrating what is possible, but following through and delivering is not a 100% guaranteed activity.

When I started ARPA-H, we wanted customers, who would be the final users of that technology, to give us feedback on what we were developing so that when we got to the last day of the experiment, they were demanding that product, versus having that be the first contact with a customer, which unfortunately is pretty common around traditional grant-making organizations.

It’s rethinking how you make sure you can transfer that knowledge off the back end of a program.

Because the folks at the lab aren’t necessarily worrying about, or prioritizing, how to make it scalable. They’re just trying to see if it works. But of course, eventually we want it to be scalable.

Sometimes the folks in the lab don’t even have the expertise or understanding of who they need to talk to next to do that, right? We think about science and those transfers as handoffs. We deploy our technology to an originating lab to understand the science and what was important about that discovery, but we can also deploy it in a receiving lab so that we can see how they’re reproducing it.

And instead of the way we transfer science today, which is looking over each other’s shoulders and saying, “Oh, you’re doing it a little wrong,” we have this video-connectedness that lets us help accelerate those iterations of transferring the science.

Do you ever get frustrated about how resources are allocated in our world? You’ve put your life toward this work, and yet so much money is devoted to, I don’t know, space exploration or the next hot social app, the Meta Muse craze. How do you deal with government and how it prioritizes things?

Yeah, it’s maddening. One of the things that has me nervous right now is that I look back on the last 80 years following the Second World War. We’ve led the globe in science and engineering and innovation. Nobody who’s practicing science today has practiced science in the United States at a time when we weren’t, quote-unquote, winning from a competitiveness perspective, when we weren’t at the top.

I genuinely believe we may lose that competitiveness, that edge, that incumbency, and I’m not sure I see us fighting for it in the way that we should be. We have to deliver on what we’ve promised to do, and that’s a commitment not just to my country, but to my kids and my family. 

What I think a lot about is Sputnik moments. We’re going to look back at this moment in time like there’s something happening, and it’s going to impact whatever’s happening 20 to 50 years from now. You can feel it in the moment.

Where that happened before, of course, was Sputnik. The United States didn’t know the Soviet Union was developing that capability, and we didn’t have a counter-capability. What I realized is that each individual person has a Sputnik moment in their life that is usually health-related. My Sputnik moment was when my mother was diagnosed with cancer. That stopped everything.

Everybody has a story, whether it happened to them or their family, or if you talk to a member of Congress, something’s happening in their state that they can’t deal with.

So I’m like, “What is the Sputnik moment now?” If ARPA-H was bringing people from an unhealthy state to a healthy state, what’s happening now is taking us beyond that. If we can figure out and solve health and wellness, a lot of people talk about abundance. What is the next trajectory? What is the Sputnik that we’re working toward?

title: FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
description:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
description: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

title: From black soldier flies to mealworms: farming insects for food, fodder and fertiliser in Uganda
description:
Cultivating the nutritious bugs means families can raise livestock and enrich their own food, while lowering pressures on the land

A few minutes’ walk from his home in the Kyaka II refugee settlement, Kanane Bikanyale feeds black soldier fly larvae to chickens in a coop above a fishpond. The larvae disappear in a scrum of chickens. Nearby, more larvae grow in modified jerrycans, while adult flies are kept in netted boxes.

Bikanyale kept chickens before he fled to Uganda from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). But the cost of conventional feed and shortages of ingredients made them increasingly difficult to raise – a widespread pressure for millions of smallholder farmers whose margins are tight.

Kanane Bikanyale tends to his black soldier fly larvae in a rearing unit in the Kyaka II refugee camp in Uganda

title: Making Room for Water: Floodable Parks in Latin America
description: Walk along a river in almost any Latin American city and you will find stretches that have been straightened, lined with concrete, buried beneath roads, or pushed behind industrial areas and residential neighborhoods. Throughout the twentieth century, urban expansion gradually occupied riverbanks and former floodplains, while waterways were redirected or confined within infrastructure intended to control them. Yet the water continued to return. For decades, flooding has been the most frequent natural disaster in Latin America and the Caribbean, according to the Inter-American Development Bank.

title: NASA's Perseverance rover drives 45.22 kilometers, sets off-world record
description:
NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles) on Mars, surpassing the 45.16-kilometer record held by the Opportunity rover, NASA said. Perseverance passed the mark on Oct. 11, its 2,006th Martian day, after about five and a half years on the planet; Opportunity took nearly 15 years to cover its distance [nasa.gov#1][sci.news#1][npr.org#1].

The rover reached the milestone while traveling toward Idubi through Lac de Charmes, near the western rim of Jezero Crater. Perseverance has collected 29 rock and soil samples and found a potential biosignature in a river-channel rock; the finding does not prove that ancient life existed on Mars [astrobiology.com#1][timeslive.co.za#1]. The crater rim may also preserve evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems, including warm or hot groundwater [dawn.com#1].

NASA has extended the rover’s mission through about the end of 2028 to continue exploring the crater rim. The vehicle’s original driving target was about 20 kilometers, and engineers are testing its mobility systems for a possible total range of 100 kilometers or more [sci.news#1][dawn.com#1]. The samples’ eventual return to Earth remains uncertain, NPR reported, citing the program’s cost and concerns raised by planetary geologist Philip Christensen [npr.org#1].

description:
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic reportedly offered a salary of 145,000 euros (roughly equal to $190,000) for a personal assistant in its London office.

The posting called for a “highly organized, detail-oriented, and self-starting administrative business partner” to support “senior go-to-market” leaders. Responsibilities would include scheduling, “handling travel logistics,” managing an executive’s inbox and communications, filing expense claims, and other office tasks.

The post, since removed from Anthropic’s website but preserved here, also stated that the role would require “outstanding attention to detail, strong relationship-building skills, and the ability to anticipate needs across teams while ensuring responsive, error-free execution.”

Fast Company reached out to Anthropic for comment.

Social media users are pointing to the apparent irony of a leading agentic AI firm hiring a human worker to do a job that an AI agent could, at least theoretically, largely handle.

“Somebody should really build some sort of tech tool that can handle this stuff autonomously,” one user quipped.

title: 3 leadership lessons from AI-powered companies
description:
Even as AI investment rises, many organizations don’t see the returns they expected. They might see small improvements by deploying AI tools into existing structures. But true success means thinking beyond the technology alone, reinventing tomorrow’s workflows, and putting AI to work for people. Our research shows only 5% of organizations are redesigning work, while others are optimizing what already exists.

When my role evolved to blend people leadership with AI enablement, it sent a clear message from our CEO: AI requires a strong people strategy at the core. I’ve seen real transformation when organizations bet on people, not just AI.

The companies unlocking results are asking the right questions about how work should change. What those leaders are learning comes down to a few key steps.

BUILD THE FOUNDATION ON DATA AND GOVERNANCE

When we rebuilt our AI HR operating model at ServiceNow, we considered how we would design it if we were starting from scratch. That helped us move from scattered pilots to a structured process with clear governance, accountability, and a way to scale without chaos.

PepsiCo’s executive vice president and chief people officer, Becky Schmitt, took a similar, structured approach. In a webinar we hosted, Schmitt a client of ours shared how she focused on data hygiene and prioritized all employees, including frontline and factory employees where safety and wellbeing are nonnegotiable.

With clean data and transparent definitions, employees can better trust and verify what AI tells them. When trust grows, adoption accelerates.

“As we’ve thought about what it means to adopt AI and harness the full power of this technology, we have five principles. Everything is human-centered. We’re fair, transparent, we have accountability, and we’re safe from the start,” she said.  

When roles are clear and processes are simple, people move faster and smarter. Governance builds confidence.

ENABLE YOUR PEOPLE WITH SKILLS THAT MATTER

By 2031, the fastest-growing technical skills will be linked to data quality, software development, analytics, and AI, according to our research. But demand for distinctly human capabilities is also accelerating.

This dual reality changes how we should think about enablement. Our client, Omar Abbosh, chief executive officer at Pearson, studies these dynamics closely. In another webinar we hosted, he said key skills that matter now are agency, learning velocity, and emotional intelligence.

Add adaptability and design thinking, and people can evolve faster than the environment shifts.

“We need to rewire occupations. We need to understand where you apply agents to specific tasks, how agents work with people, and how people can supervise and orchestrate. That level of rewiring results in a new operating model. It’s process, it’s systems, and it’s the motivation required to change the culture,” he said in the webinar.

But you can’t teach these skills in a classroom. Real-time learning embedded in daily work beats traditional reskilling programs. We give our employees personalized learning recommendations tailored to how AI will be used in their roles, which allows them to understand the why behind its use and the value of human judgment in their work. We have seen that when you coach people through the work they’re doing, learning is faster, stickier, and more scalable.

TRANSFORM THE WORKFORCE WITH CHANGE READINESS 

AI adoption is increasing, yet many people aren’t aware of their organization’s AI strategy. This is a disconnect that leaders need to address with continuous, adaptive, and decentralized change readiness.

This is often the hardest part of a transformation because it’s complex and abstract. It’s about changing the way we work at a fundamental level, which requires a strong understanding of your organization’s structure and capabilities. And it requires keeping employees informed about the skills the organization is prioritizing, how roles are evolving, and the path forward.

Another client of ours, Nickle LaMoreaux, senior vice president and chief human resources officer at IBM, used an “X-Ray” framework as a foundation to rethink her organization with an AI-native mindset. As she explained in a different webinar we hosted, “We were really clear from the beginning that we were going to put employees at the center of this.”

By recognizing the importance of redesigning jobs and helping employees feel comfortable with the technology, Nickle built a powerful model to map current skills against future needs.

Her team also identified where redesign was most urgent. Then, IBM shared that analysis with employees.

“You have to redesign jobs. If you wait too long, you can quickly fall behind, especially at the pace things are moving today. When we talk about redesigning jobs, we need to shift our thinking from the job as a whole to the tasks and skills underneath it,” she said.

That kind of analysis can help leaders think about future skills as AI changes work. The end goal is a workforce that can pivot at the speed of innovation. It’s about shifting the mindset to “let’s try this” instead of “don’t break this.”

THE FLYWHEEL

We’ve been through big technology shifts before. AI transformation feels different because of the pace, but those examples should give us confidence.

title: The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth
description:
Steve Martin’s favorite comic moment of his entire career is the “hamburger” scene from The Pink Panther (2006), he once told People magazine. Martin plays Inspector Clouseau, who has an aggressively exaggerated French accent. In the scene, he is trying to learn how to say, “I would like to buy a hamburger,” with a dialect coach. “Dam-buergaaaaa,” he purrs at his coach, along with increasingly ridiculous permutations of all of the other words in the sentence.

The scene is funny because it’s true for so many of us: Learning a new language as an adult can be hard. The unfamiliar sounds may get tangled up in the mouth like marbles, and the results can sound like gibberish. But for other people, new foreign words seem to roll off the tongue and adopting different accents comes easily. Their secret may lie in how they listen, according to a new study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology. People who are better at detecting small differences in the frequency of raw sound are better at picking up new foreign speech sounds, and thus might be quicker to learn new languages, the study found.

“Read more: Speaking More Languages May Help Slow Brain Aging”

The post The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth appeared first on Nautilus.

title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
description:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.

The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.

title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.

By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.

title: Mexico City Architecture City Guide: 38 Projects From Tenochtitlan to the 21st Century
description: Mexico City is a sprawling metropolis of layered temporalities, where architecture operates as a continuous negotiation between deep-seated history and intense urban mutation. Built over the aquatic traces of Tenochtitlan, the city's fabric is an ongoing dialogue between eras: the monumental scale of the Pre-Hispanic Templo Mayor and the Viceroyalty architecture of the Catedral Metropolitana coexist with the modern and contemporary impulses that define its skyline. This dense juxtaposition creates a unique urban canvas where sacred geography, colonial imposition, and 20th-century ambition intersect.

title: As a domestic car sales slump continues, China’s automakers lean on exports
description:
China’s passenger car exports surged 64% in September from the same month in 2025, an industry association reported Monday, as Chinese automakers increasingly focus on exports to drive growth amid sluggish domestic sales.

China exported around 919,000 passenger vehicles in September, lifted by overseas demand for plug-in hybrids and pure electric vehicles, data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers showed. In the first nine months of 2026, China exported over 7.1 million passenger cars, up more than 70% from the same period last year.

Meanwhile, domestic passenger car sales in China fell for most of the year as automakers faced weaker consumer confidence at home and scaled-back government subsidies. They fell 27% year over year in September to over 1.6 million units, according to the association.

China is the world’s largest vehicle exporter, but is facing increasing skepticism from trade partners who fear it’s undermining their domestic industries and trade balance.

The European Union is capping Chinese hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 a year, officials say.

Chinese car sales grow in regions including Europe

In recent months, Chinese automakers have more aggressively targeted rapid growth in overseas markets such as Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and Africa. Canada is also opening its doors to Chinese EV exports under a tariff cut deal with China.

The industry increasingly relies on overseas markets for sales and profit growth as players seek to offset weakness in the domestic market, analyst Stephen Chan of S&P Global Ratings said.

Consultancy AlixPartners and some auto analysts expect Chinese automakers to export nearly or around 10 million vehicles globally in 2026.

In Europe, Chinese automakers are increasingly challenging the European auto industry with lower costs and prices. AlixPartners’ analysis found, for example, that a Chinese-branded EV costs around $20,000 to produce, compared with $31,000 for a European equivalent.

EU to cap Chinese hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 annually

The EU has already imposed higher tariffs on pure electric vehicles from China, prompting Chinese carmakers to export more hybrid vehicles. Recent policy discussions have focused on the rapid rise in sales of Chinese hybrids in Europe.

Chinese automakers captured around 12% of Europe’s new-car market in August and accounted for one in four hybrid sales in the region, said a research note by Deutsche Bank.

Amid growing pressure on the EU to rebalance trade with China, EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič said Friday that the two sides had reached an interim deal that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc.

The agreement sets an annual import quota of 350,000 hybrid vehicles made in China, including plug-in hybrids, two senior EU officials said Monday. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity under European Commission policy.

Starting as early as December, customs authorities across the 27-nation bloc will coordinate monitoring of these imports and halt further shipments once the annual quota is reached, one official said. The limit excludes cars made in Europe by Chinese companies.

Analysts said protectionist measures would likely continue to cloud Chinese automakers’ overseas outlook.

An import cap on Chinese hybrid cars would likely disrupt the highly profitable vehicle export growth that Chinese automakers recently enjoyed in the European market, Deutsche Bank analysts said.

“You can’t expect BYD or the other OEMs [original equipment manufacturers] to export too many cars without facing tariffs or pushbacks from the foreign governments,” Xiao Feng, head of Hong Kong and China industrials research at investment group CITIC CLSA, told reporters recently.

Geopolitics is the biggest challenge to BYD’s overseas expansion, executive vice president Stella Li, who leads the Chinese EV giant’s global growth, acknowledged at an event this month.

BYD has therefore been expanding overseas production, including setting up plants in Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, and Hungary, she told the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore.

More overseas production limits impact from trade curbs

Chinese automakers will likely continue to expand overseas production to reduce exposure to tariffs and other risks, said Ming Lee, head of Greater China automotive and industrial research at BofA Global Research, a unit of Bank of America.

“More and more volume will be made locally,” he said.

Meanwhile, the U.S. has effectively shut Chinese EVs out of its market with hefty tariffs. President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during Xi’s state visit to Washington last month yielded no deal on access for Chinese EVs.

Experts say continued political uncertainty likely makes the U.S. market a lower priority for Chinese automakers.

—By Chan Ho-Him and Sam McNeil, Associated Press

title: When your AI system breaks—and what to do about it
description:
The announcement of a new AI model or feature fills me with a mixture of anticipation and dread. I’m excited to see what “new thing” I might be able to do, but I also know that some of my existing processes and systems might break as a result.

Every AI tool comes with the disclaimer that it can make mistakes. You might set up a workflow that is perfectly fine one day and perfectly awful the next. 

It’s an ongoing challenge. Unlike traditional software, once an AI system is up and running, it’s not set-it-and-forget-it. Even a system that seems to be working fine needs an occasional check-in or fine-tuning.

The predictable AI failures

AI can stop working in some very predictable ways. Maybe it’s connected to an external tool (like your email), and the connection expired. Some AI tools require your computer to be on/awake for tasks to run. You might get an error message, or the output never shows up. 

These failures are easy to address because it’s often clear what went awry. You reconnect and try again. 

I rely heavily on AI scheduled tasks and have a notification system built in. If something breaks, I get an email telling me to review the process. That way, I realize immediately that something went wrong and can fix it. 

The unpredictable AI failures

The harder failure is when an AI process runs as expected, but the output gets worse. Models and functionality change almost daily. You may have a well-crafted prompt that gave you what you were looking for last month, but the results are noticeably different today. 

People in the industry call this “drift.” Most setups have no way to catch it, since technically nothing broke.

I use Claude and struggled with Opus 5.0. For the way I use AI, the output was “off” in a way I couldn’t quite put my finger on. I found myself returning to Opus 4.6, which was the last model where I felt comfortable. (As an aside: the update to Opus 5.5 went much more smoothly.)

The most reliable way to catch drift is to consistently review AI output, no matter how long it has been working as expected. Give every review the same critical eye you gave it the first time you tested an AI process. 

Drift is inconvenient, especially when the whole point of an automation is to save you time. But you can’t count on a model to behave the same way from one month to the next. I look at it this way: a 5-minute review is still faster than the 20-30 minutes it may have taken me to do the task manually. 

Factor ‘AI maintenance’ into your routine

AI tools save me a lot of time. But keeping my prompts and processes working smoothly takes time, too. That time has to come from somewhere.

Some fixes can’t wait. When a notification tells me something failed, I often need to look at it right away. Depending on what broke, it can throw off my whole workflow until I fix it. 

Other changes I have to set aside time to review thoroughly. When a new model is announced, I don’t switch over right away. A big change in output could derail an afternoon, so I take time to test it first.

Upkeep is part of the cost of any AI system you set up. And if a process takes more time to maintain than it saves you, it’s fair to ask whether it’s worth keeping.

Tech Week is in full bloom in San Francisco, packing the city’s restaurants this week with venture capitalists and AI founders ebullient about the White House’s stance on regulating artificial intelligence — namely, don’t do it.

And after months of debate about leading AI companies’ unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data, the nation now finds itself further from governing AI systems than it was a few years ago.

President Donald Trump brought tech titans to Washington late last month for a luncheon and ceremonial signing of a voluntary safety pact he described as “almost a constitution” surrounding “Super Intelligence,” the administration’s new preferred term for AI.

The 308-word agreement lays out that advanced AI labs should follow safety protocols and set up internal teams to monitor their own progress, but the administration has yet to provide details on how, in OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s words, to keep “bad things” from happening.

Safety challenges were not top of mind inside a crowded event space in San Francisco on Wednesday, where founders and funders said the government’s hands-off approach would net higher profits for companies building AI-powered defense and security systems.

Panelists praised the government’s bullish industry support at one meeting aimed at “investing in the forefront,” part of the blitz of popup events organized by Andreessen Horowitz, a venture firm whose head is a Trump science and tech adviser.

“I want to start with one figure that I think really emphasizes the investment opportunity of defense, and that’s $1 trillion. The U.S. government, for the first time, is allocating $1 trillion to its defense spending. And $13.5 billion of that will go to autonomous systems and AI,” said Kyle Stanford, a venture capital research director at PitchBook, a market intelligence platform. “That has obviously brought a lot of capital into defense tech spending, more than we’ve ever seen.”

New concerns emerge on AI safety

A day later, three researchers at OpenAI’s headquarters said the ChatGPT maker had fired them, posting that “fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work.” Separately, David Robinson, a leader on OpenAI’s safety team until he recently resigned, said he was worried about letting the advanced labs police themselves.

“This is no substitute for hard law, and it does give a lot of freedom to the companies,” Robinson said. “The time between model generations is measured in weeks … and I think we have some very serious safety challenges in front of us in the nearer term.”

Trump has staked his political capital on the AI industry’s success, saying its unbridled development is key to winning the AI race against China. On the first day of his second term, the Republican president repealed a Biden-era executive order aimed in part at guarding against the risks that AI systems pose to consumers, workers and national security.

His administration has since reoriented federal policy away from oversight and toward rapid growth, including by canceling previous requirements for AI developers to share safety test results with the federal government. In December, Trump signed an executive order aimed at blocking AI regulations at the state level, saying a patchwork of rules could stifle the industry.

Even as Silicon Valley companies have disclosed their models’ involvement in troubling cyberattacks throughout the year, the burgeoning tech sector has continued to drive economic growth.

Concerns about AI safety centered on existential risk, rather than current real-world harms, landed at the center of debates last month, when a relatively unknown Anthropic engineer quit and called for a pause on tech development to keep “superhuman” systems from eluding controls. Then, Anthropic and OpenAI CEOs echoed the call to slow AI development. To some critics, their public manifestos appeared aimed at currying favor with investors ahead of their public listings and the midterm elections, when the political tides could turn with many voters opposed to data centers.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump posted in response on Truth Social, warning voters not to “kill the Golden Goose,” a term he has used to refer to both AI and data centers.

White House pact preserves wide latitude for AI companies

As calls mounted for stricter control of AI, the administration brought tech executives to the White House for lunch, followed by a ceremonial signing of the agreement on AI safety.

“I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters after the event.

The document was signed by representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, SpaceXAI and Nvidia.

OpenAI is committed to embedding external assessors and finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors, said a spokesperson, who referred AP to a company post stating that the researchers were fired for violating “clear policies on handling sensitive information.”

Google referred to CEO Sundar Pichai’s post that the company does appropriate testing and evaluations and is collaborating “to establish norms and build public confidence.”

Meta recently updated its standards for training, evaluating and releasing its most capable AI models, and spokesman Andy Stone pointed to the company’s efforts to refine its board of directors’ governance structure.

Nvidia and SpaceXAI did not respond to requests for comment.

Anthropic, which voluntarily disclosed Friday that its agents submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, is bringing in independent evaluators and discussing collaborations with industry groups, a spokesperson said.

In a statement, the White House reiterated Trump’s comments about working with industry to balance innovation and security and did not directly answer questions about how the administration plans to monitor the AI companies’ implementation.

Following the new Anthropic disclosure, it added that the Trump administration expected full transparency from the company, saying notification and remediation was “not optional. It is a critical national security obligation.”

Under Democratic President Joe Biden, leading AI companies also made voluntary commitments to promote “safe, secure, and transparent development” of their models that included specific guidelines for tests and transparency reports. The current accord lacks that, said Sarah Myers West, a former senior AI adviser to the Federal Trade Commission.

“Across the board, this self-regulatory approach has consistently done one thing, which is failed to work. It’s failed to in any meaningful way ensure that these companies are honestly even keeping their house in order, let alone ensuring that they are compliant with existing law,” said Myers West, now co-executive director of the New York-based nonprofit AI Now. “All that they’re getting is grace from this government.”

After last month’s luncheon with Trump, the FTC said it had opened an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies over dangers their technology may pose to consumers. The FTC didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump recently appointed National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson to serve on his new “Super Intelligence Force,” which the president said would keep the U.S. dominant in AI development. He posted Thursday that the White House would consider anyone who does not refer to AI using his preferred term as “THE ENEMY!”

Members of Congress, as well as civil liberties and consumer rights groups, have pushed for more regulations on AI, saying there is not enough oversight.

Graham Steele, a former assistant secretary in the U.S. Treasury Department, said even if AI companies set up internal evaluation teams or hire outside evaluators, such a structure can make them vulnerable to undue pressure on their work.

“We live in a democratic society. Are they the right ones to have the power to be able to make decisions that have broad, structural, social, and political consequences?” Steele said.

—Garance Burke, Associated Press

title: Tim Cook Visits China for the Third Time in 2026
description:
Tim Cook is visiting China for the third time this year, with talks in Guangdong focused on expanding Apple's manufacturing and sales operations, the South China Morning Post reports.



This is Cook's first China trip in his capacity as Apple's executive chairman. He moved into the position on September 1 when John Ternus took over as CEO. Apple has said part of Cook's work involves relationships with government policymakers.

On October 11, Cook reportedly held talks with Guangdong governor Meng Fanli. Suppliers and partners located in Guangdong play a major role in Apple's business in China, and Cook is said to have expressed interest in doing more locally through smart manufacturing and additional sales channels. Meng said the province would support further expansion, including research and development.

In Guangzhou, a creator used an iPhone 18 Pro to capture martial arts footage while Cook watched. Cook posted "Great to be back in China!" on Weibo on Saturday. Customers also reported a visit to one of Guangzhou's Apple Stores on Sunday.

Cook traveled to Chengdu and Beijing in March as Apple celebrated its 50th anniversary, and addressed the China Development Forum. In May, he was among the business leaders who accompanied President Donald Trump for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The trip comes several weeks after sales of the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max started. Counterpoint Research put Apple first in China's smartphone sales ranking for September 14 to 20. During their first three days on sale in China, the new Pro phones sold 12% more units than their predecessors had managed over the full first week of availability last year.
Tags: China, South China Morning Post, Tim Cook

This article, "Tim Cook Visits China for the Third Time in 2026" first appeared on MacRumors.com

title: How AI can prevent knowledge from walking out the door
description:
Knowledge is what separates a good operation from a great one. It is also the hardest thing to scale, because the knowledge that matters most does not live in systems. It lives in people. The team member who knows that this client needs a call before a decision, not after. The leader who has seen this pattern before and knows where it breaks. The analyst who understands why the model is wrong this time even when the numbers say otherwise. That knowledge compounds when it stays and disappears when people leave; training and documentation rarely capture it. Agentic operations changes that equation.

A DIFFERENT KIND OF WORK

Automation means rules. If the task matches the template, proceed. That is useful, but rules are static and the real world is not. The moment a case falls outside the template, the automation stops.

Agentic operations rooted in process intelligence operates differently. In an enterprise, every task sits inside a workflow of decisions, exceptions, and approvals. Process intelligence maps that workflow as it really runs, not as the manual describes it, and holds it as a living, machine-readable knowledge graph.

Capturing judgment is the harder part, and it is a discipline of its own. It begins where the work deviates from the procedure: the overrides, escalations, and exceptions resolved differently than the playbook says. Those are the moments where experience is doing the work. The next step is to recover the reasoning behind each one. What did the expert notice? What did they weigh? What did they know about this customer, supplier, and time of year that the system did not? That reasoning is tied to the context in which it applied and tested against historical cases to see whether it holds. Only then does it become part of the graph. What gets encoded is a reasoned pattern: in this situation, for this reason, the answer tends to be this.

With that in place, the agent can read a situation and reason through it. The agent can know when to decide, when to ask for input, and when to hand over to a human expert in a governed workflow. It then executes, plans, decides, and acts across the end-to-end process. When a human steps in, the decision and the reasoning behind it flow back into the graph, so the next decision is better informed than the last.

The work that has always resisted automation is judgment work. That includes exceptions and edge cases, the moments where context determines the right answer and no rule exists. This is where agentic operations are built to work.

THE LAST MILE

There is a point in every process where the gap between what experienced people know and what the system knows becomes consequential. A shipment arrives three days late, affecting downstream commitments. A new customer does not fit the standard profile. A decision falls outside the defined threshold, and someone has to determine what it means. This is the last mile. It is where consequences are real, where trust is built or broken, and where generic tools consistently fall short.

Most AI deployments handle the routine work and hand these moments back to humans. A well-designed agent works at that boundary. It executes end-to-end, surfaces uncertainty, and routes the decision to the right person with the right context. Then it encodes what it learned. Every exception teaches the system, and every deployment makes the next one more precise.

The experienced team member who once spent the day reviewing routine work now spends it on decisions that require judgment. New team members inherit context that took years to build. The floor rises for everyone.

SPECIFICITY IS THE PRIZE

When a system holds the reasoning behind a decision, not just the rule, it applies that reasoning differently depending on context. It knows what this customer needs based on everything that has come before. It knows where this process tends to break, and why. It flags the anomaly because it understands what normal looks like in this specific environment. An organization can serve more markets, more customers, and more complexity with more precision than it could before. The quality of the relationship does not erode as the operation scales. It deepens, because the system carries the context that once required a person to hold it.

But this only works if agentic operations are built on real operational knowledge. Frontier models are great. But they cannot tell you how your specific operation runs, where it breaks under real conditions, or what your most important customers need that your standard process does not capture. That knowledge has to be engineered in. It takes years to build and cannot be purchased. That is the work of process intelligence.

There is no artificial intelligence without process intelligence. Deploy without it and you automate the operation without the intelligence that makes it work. Build with it and your advantage compounds.

Balkrishan “BK” Kalra is president and CEO of Genpact.

title: Transcriptomic Approaches to Guiding the Discovery of Geroprotective Compounds
description: A great deal of drug discovery starts by screening compounds from the vast libraries of molecules that exist. The libraries are too large to screen everything (and even then the scope of the libraries is only a sampling of the space of the possible). Thus even unbiased screening starts with some hypothesis to cut down the number of molecules being screened to a tractable number for the time and budget at hand. Here, researchers discuss the use of existing transcriptomic data to guide drug screening approaches intended to uncover geroprotective compounds that adjust metabolism to modestly slow aging. Based on results to date, this side of aging research seems unlikely to produce exciting outcomes, as near all of what has been discovered in this way […]

title: The Cultural Life of Colors in Latin American Interiors
description: A color has a biography. A color can have an origin, but it can also transform. It can move between materials and disciplines, from a local practice into architecture, from something ordinary into something symbolic. It can lose one association and acquire another, or persist without anyone consciously thinking of it as cultural. Its life unfolds through the conditions in which it is produced, used, repeated, and inhabited. As these conditions change, so do the meanings a color can carry.

title: "A Place Remembers What Has Happened:" Tsuyoshi Tane on Memory as a Design Driver in Louisiana Channel Interview
description: Tsuyoshi Tane is a Japanese architect born in 1979 in Tokyo and based in Paris, where he founded ATTA – Atelier Tsuyoshi Tane Architects in 2006. Working across cultural, institutional, and landscape-related projects, Tane has developed an architectural approach that positions memory as a fundamental design driver. In his interview with Louisiana Channel, filmed in his Paris studio, Tane reflects on architecture as a discipline of observation and thought, arguing that meaningful design emerges from carefully reading the traces embedded within a site. For him, architecture is not produced on a blank slate but begins with an inquiry into what already exists, physically, culturally, and emotionally, beneath the surface of a place.

description: Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.

title: “Cities Are Mental Weapons”: Utopian Hours 2026 Returns to Turin with Sir Peter Cook and a Program on City-Making
description: The second part of the Utopian Hours 2026 international city-making festival will be held in Turin on October 16 and 17. After a first chapter in Rotterdam, the festival is marking its tenth anniversary edition by returning to its hometown in Italy. The event's lineup and cultural program are designed to explore how cities can respond creatively to the social, environmental, and political challenges of the 21st century. The Utopian Hours festival has been organized since 2017 by Stratosferica, a nonprofit cultural association dedicated to producing and sharing urban knowledge through content on the evolution of cities, urban communication strategies, events, community building and placemaking.

=== 19th Century ===
After incorporation of Houston in 1837, the Second Ward was established as one of the original four wards of Houston through charter statutes passed in 1839 and 1840. The boundaries of the Second Ward were Buffalo Bayou to the north, Main Street to the west, Congress Avenue to the south, and the city limits to the east. The Second Ward elected two aldermen to represent them in municipal government.<ref>{{cite journal | first=Betty Trapp | last=Chapman | journal=Houston History Magazine | page=30 | url=https://houstonhistorymagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/ward-system-of-government.pdf | access-date=July 25, 2025 | volume=8 | issue=1 |year=2010 | title=A System of Government Where Business Ruled}}</ref>

By 1860, the Second Ward included some of the wealthiest people in Houston. [[William J. Hutchins]] and [[William Marsh Rice]] each reported wealth of at least $700,000 to the census taker in 1860. In addition to these wealthy residents who resided in town between Franklin and Congress avenues, Robert Lockhart and John T. Brady lived in remote neighborhoods, far east in the Second Ward. Lockhart was a merchant and grist mill owner who married into the [[Francis Lubbock]] family, and resided on a large homestead known as "Lubbock's Grove." Brady, another wealthy Second Ward resident, was an attorney, state legislator, and investor.<ref>McWhorter (2010), pp. 38−39.</ref>

By the late nineteenth century Second Ward had a heavily [[German American]] community. Thomas McWhorter, author of "From Das Zweiter to El Segundo, A Brief History of Houston’s Second Ward," wrote that "Second Ward became an unofficial hub of German-American culture and social life."<ref name=McWhorterp40>McWhorter (2010), p. 40.</ref> The Houston [[Saengerbund]] was established in 1883 as a German-American singing group, one of many that proliferated in the [[German diaspora]] during that era. It bought the William Hamblen House in 1913. It was the final German American cultural organization to be established in the Second Ward.<ref name="McWhorterp41" /> The Houston Saengerbund left the Second Ward in 1935.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.houstonsaengerbund.org/site/about/history/|title=History|publisher=Houston Saengerbund|accessdate=2022-10-15}}</ref> In the late 1800s Volksfest Park hosted the Volkfest festival, a German-American event. Its attendance prompted the Bayou Street Railway Company to, in 1889, add a [[mule car]] line to the park.<ref>McWhorter p. 40-41.</ref>The German community and organizations were suppressed during [[World War I]] and its resulting [[anti-German sentiment]]. In 1992 former [[Mayor of Houston]] [[Bob Lanier (politician)|Bob Lanier]] proposed converting the {{convert|10.5|acre|m2|adj=on}} former Milby Bus Barn site into a 59-family low income development which would have been called La Villa de las Flores ([[Spanish language|Spanish]] for "the Village of the Flowers"); the [[Metropolitan Transit Authority of Harris County, Texas]] used the site as a bus barn from 1976 to 1983. In 1993 workers doing preliminary jobs discovered unused storage tanks, prompting testing for dangerous chemicals. Soil tests revealed petroleum and lead; the lead was 300 times the amount of safe concentration for a homeowner. Local residents received testing. title: Visualizing crossbeam Epoch Based Reclamation
description:
In my previous post we experienced first hand the horrors that can occur when attempting to use lock-free data structures with pointers. We left the question of how to deal with this problem a bit open.

Languages like Java with a garbage collector don’t have this issue, since the runtime collects the memory when it’s unreachable by all threads. I recently learned that one of the ways to solve this in a deterministic manner in Rust is through a method called Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR), which the crate crossbeam-epoch implements. My goal is not to explain the theoretical concepts, as that endeavour has been already been accomplished by Aaron Turon, the founder of Crossbeam.

Instead, as I’ve done in previous posts, I want to dissect and visualize what exactly is going on. If that sounds fun, you’re welcome to come along for the ride!

I can also recommend another pleasant read that demonstrates the usage of crossbeam-epoch.

You can access the code used in this post.

Q1: When to Drop

We looked at the buggy implementation of a lock-free stack and managed to reproduce the ABA bug. Here’s a diagram for a quick recap:

The fundamental question is:

  1. How do we defer drop() until Thread A is no longer reading it, without adding locks or atomic reference counter updates on every single read?

Q2: Updating Pointer and Flag Atomically

Another important question also comes up when removing a node requires two steps. This is the case when working with lock-free linked lists. Check out Timothy Harris’ Paper for a more detailed explanation of this algorithm. Essentially, deleting is done in two parts:

  1. Mark the node as deleted (or more specifically, it’s next pointer) so other threads don’t try to insert after it.
  2. Physically unlink it via CAS.

There’s a limit set by the hardware that normal CPU atomic instructions can only swap one word (64 bits) at a time. We can’t swap a next pointer and a separate is_deleted: bool flag atomically. This raises a second question, namely:

  1. How do we atomically update both a pointer and a state flag in a single CAS instruction, without a double-word atomic write?

Motivation and Goal

When I started writing this, I had planned for just one post visualizing the ABA bug and then analyzing how crossbeam solves it. However, I quickly realized it was too much to pack into just one post, and the ABA problem deserved its own post. Then, as I was writing this continuation, I initially just cared about Q1. However, I came across something that I found really awesome (don’t want to spoil the next section), and I wondered why do we need it… so that’s how I came to Q2, and I couldn’t just leave it out. In the meantime, I was playing around with Loom, so that became its own post. So far in the series:

  • Part 1: Visualizing The ABA Problem: What crossbeam-epoch Solves
  • Part 2: Using Loom to (Try To) Catch an ABA Bug in Lock-Free Rust
  • Part 3: current

Without further ado, the goal of this post is to dissect crossbeam-epoch to better understand how it solves Q1 and Q2.

Q2: Dissecting crossbeam::epoch::Shared

To give a refresher, the building blocks of crossbeam-epoch are:

crossbeam type analogue role
Owned<T> Box<T> Unique, non-atomic ownership.
Atomic<T> AtomicPtr<T> Shared, atomic location.
Shared<'a, T> &'g T Borrowed reference tied to a Guard.

The Owned<T> holds heap allocated data that isn’t shared yet. You turn an Owned into a Shared or store it inside an Atomic.

Atomic<T> is what you’ll use in your data structures. It holds a pointer that can be updated using CAS (Compare-And-Swap) or other atomic operations.

Shared<'a, T> is obtained by calling .load(&guard) on an Atomic. The lifetime 'g guarantees the pointer cannot be freed by another thread as long as your pin() guard is alive. (We’ll discuss this later).

Using Wasted Alignment Bits for Metadata

Every type has an alignment requirement. We can imagine that memory is organized in “shelves,” where each variable must sit. This way, you can’t have a variable sitting in between two shelves. Each type has its own alignment requirement (shelf size). In modern 64-bit architectures, a pointer requires 8-byte alignment.

For a type T with 8-byte alignment, every valid pointer to a T is a multiple of 8. If you look at memory addresses that are multiples of 8 in binary, you can see that the lowest 3 bits are in a sense “wasted.” They don’t hold any other useful information, since they’re guaranteed to be always 000.

Decimal Address Hex Address 64-bit Binary Address (Lowest Byte)
16 0x0010 … 0001 0000
24 0x0018 … 0001 1000
32 0x0020 … 0010 0000
40 0x0028 … 0010 1000

You can believe this was my face when I learned what crossbeam does with this information.

Crossbeam reclaims those unused low-order bits to store some metadata directly inside the pointer value.

For reading or dereferencing the pointer, crossbeam masks out those bits using bitwise AND to reconstruct the valid address:

Original Address = Raw Pointer & ~ Tag Mask

This is purely awesome. We can store a small piece of metadata, like a “deleted” mark, directly inside the pointer itself. So the pointer and the flag can be updated together in a single CAS, without needing a separate variable.

Taking a Look Inside

To work with crossbeam-epoch, we first allocate data on the heap using Owned<T> (similar to Box<T>). We then transfer this pointer into an Atomic<T> location. This enables us to share it across threads.

Before reading from the Atomic<T>, a thread must pin the current global epoch. We’ll discuss this in a bit, but basically we’re announcing that this thread is actively working with memory, and for as long as this Guard lives, other threads aren’t allowed to drop the object(s) we’re working with. This guaranntees that any Shared<'a, T> references we have remain safe to dereference.

let node = Owned::new(Node { data: 42 } );
let atomic_ptr = Atomic::from(node);

let guard = &epoch::pin();

let shared_ptr = atomic_ptr.load(Ordering::Acquire, guard);

Now that we have our Shared<'a, T> we can play around with it, changing the tag and verifying what happens in memory:

  1. Show initial state: tag is 0.
 println!("Initial tag: {}", shared_ptr.tag());
 println!("Initial address: {:#018x} --> last byte: {:08b}", shared_ptr.as_raw() as usize, shared_ptr.as_raw() as usize & 0xFF);
 println!("----------------------------------");
  1. Set tag to 2. with_tag creates a new Shared pointer with updated tag bits.
 let tagged_ptr_2 = shared_ptr.with_tag(2);
 let raw_bits_2 = unsafe { std::mem::transmute::<_, usize>(tagged_ptr_2) };

 println!("Tag: {}", tagged_ptr_2.tag());
 println!("Tagged address (tag 2): {:#018x} --> last byte: {:08b}", &raw_bits_2, &raw_bits_2);
 println!("tagged_ptr_2.as_raw(): {:#018x}", tagged_ptr_2.as_raw() as usize);
 println!("----------------------------------");
  1. Update tag to 3.
 let tagged_ptr_3 = tagged_ptr_2.with_tag(3);
 let raw_bits_3 = unsafe { std::mem::transmute::<_, usize>(tagged_ptr_3) };

 println!("Tag: {}", tagged_ptr_3.tag());
 println!("Tagged address (tag 3): {:#018x} --> last byte: {:08b}", &raw_bits_3, &raw_bits_3 & 0xFF);
 println!("tagged_ptr_3.as_raw(): {:#018x}", tagged_ptr_3.as_raw() as usize);
 println!("----------------------------------");
  1. Verify that dereferencing ignores tag bits.
 let node_ref: &Node = unsafe { tagged_ptr_3.deref() };
 let physical_addr = (node_ref as *const Node) as usize;

 println!("Clean Physical Address: {:#018x}", physical_addr);
 println!("Node inner data: {}", node_ref.data);

Let’s run it:


Initial tag: 0
Initial address: 0x000056065369dd50 --> last byte: 01010000
----------------------------------
Tag: 2
Tagged address (tag 2): 0x000056065369dd52 --> last byte: 01010010
tagged_ptr_2.as_raw(): 0x000056065369dd50
----------------------------------
Tag: 3
Tagged address (tag 3): 0x000056065369dd53 --> last byte: 01010011
tagged_ptr_3.as_raw(): 0x000056065369dd50
----------------------------------
Clean Physical Address: 0x000056065369dd50
Node inner data: 42

This answers our second question, let’s now tackle the first one:

  1. How do we defer drop() until Thread A is no longer reading it, without adding locks or atomic reference counter updates on every single read?

  2. How do we atomically update both a pointer and a state flag in a single CAS instruction, without a double-word atomic write?

Q1: Visualizing When a Node Gets Dropped

Now for the first and most awaited question: how does crossbeam-epoch delay drop() until no thread is reading the node?

The idea of epoch-based reclamation was first introduced by Keir Fraser in his PhD thesis, and what a beautiful concept it is! The first implementation of crossbeam-epoch was written by Aaron Turon and the approach is described beautifully in his blog. Please check that out beforehand if it’s your first time exploring this concept, since I don’t go too deep here, just a recap before jumping into the visualization experiment.

Epoch-Based Reclamation Quick Recap

To recap, the global epoch is a mod 3 counter. When a thread wants to access memory, it “pins” itself to the current epoch (it essentially records the epoch it saw when it was pinned). The epoch can advance from e to e + 1 if every pinned thread has already “observed” e. When a thread retires a node (unlinks it from the data structure), it goes into a “bin” labeled with the current epoch.

Why we need only 3 “bins”?

My first question when reading about this was “why only 3 epochs”? And the explanation is actually extremely elegant, very clever.

  • Bin e (current): Unsafe to free. Threads pinned at e may have loaded the pointer just before it was unlinked and could still be reading it.
  • Bin e - 1: Unsafe to free. Threads can be pinned at e - 1 still, since the epoch advanced once everyone had observed e - 1. This check didn’t require them to have moved on. This means that such threads could still hold a pointer to something unlinked in e - 1.
  • Bin e - 2: Safe to free. For the epoch to get from e - 2 to e, it had to pass from e - 1 to e, which required that every pinned thread be at e - 1 or later. This guarantees that nobody is still at e - 2. Anyone who could have had a pointer to the node (pinned at e - 2 or earlier, since it was unlinked at e - 2) has since unpinned or re-pinned, and can’t hold that pointer.

This is the theoretical explanation. As for crossbeam, it doesn’t literally keep 3 bins. Each thread has a local bag. “Sealed” bags go into a global queue marked with the corresponding epoch. A bag is freed once the global epoch is at least two ahead of the bag’s mark. The global epoch itself behaves like a mod 3 counter, but is a plain increasing counter. This makes a lot more sense with the diagram!

Experiment #1: Pinned Thread Prevents Drop

To visualize what exactly it looks like in action, we can use a custom collector. Normally, every 128th call to pin() on a thread automatically triggers a garbage collection attempt (try_advance()). However, in order to control when this happens, we can use a custom collector and explicitly call .flush().

For EBR, a “thread” is just a registered handle. Handles aren’t even required to live on different OS threads, so we can play T1 and T2 from a single thread, just for demonstration purposes.

We can create a custom type that flips a flag when it is dropped. (This flag lives in an Arc, and our object holds a clone to that Arc, so we can still access the flag once the object dies).

struct DropTracker {
 flag: Arc<AtomicBool>,
}

impl Drop for DropTracker {
 fn drop(&mut self) {
 self.flag.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst);
 }
}

We create a custom collector and register two handles, which simulate threads, T1 and T2.

let collector = Collector::new();
let (t1, t2) = (collector.register(), collector.register());

Create instances of the DropTracker holding an Arc containing the flag.

let flag = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));

let tracker = Atomic::new(DropTracker {
 flag: flag.clone()
});

T1 pins, receiving a Guard:

let g1 = t1.pin();

T2 unlinks the value and retires it:

{
 let guard2 = t2.pin();
 let old = tracker.swap(Shared::null(), Ordering::AcqRel, &guard2);

 // defer_destroy is unsafe because the compiler can't
 // verify that nodoby can still reach the pointer
 // Safety: we know nobody can reach the pointer anymore
 // because we've "unlinked" it from our data structure
 unsafe { guard2.defer_destroy(old) };
} // guard2 gets dropped

If we go back to our stack situation, this would be analogous to when T2 pops node A and then drops it. With EBR, instead of dropping it right away, it goes into T2’s garbage bag. It can’t be cleaned up while T1’s guard is still alive. By holding this guard, it stops the global epoch from advancing. The bag only expires once the epoch has moved on.

This only protects threads reading tracker who pinned it before it was unlinked (swaped out). What happens if a thread pins afterward? In this case, that thread cannot see this node anymore because we’ve already unlinked it from our data structure (or swaped it out, in this case).

Now, while T1’s Guard is still alive, we try to manually trigger the garbage collection by calling .flush() a couple of times:

let mut flushes = 0;

while !flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) && flushes < 5 {
 // why do we need a fresh pin every time?
 t2.pin().flush();

 flushes += 1;
 println!("flush #{flushes}: flag = {}", flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst));
}

Side note: Why do we need a fresh pin every time for T2?

We need a fresh pin() for T2 every time we try this because Guard records the epoch it was pinned at, and that is the value that try_advance checks. If T2 were to keep one guard alive across flushes, T2 itself becomes the lagging thread blocking the epoch.

We’ll see that until we drop T1’s Guard, our tracker doesn’t get dropped, no matter how many times we try to flush().

flush #1: flag = false
flush #2: flag = false
flush #3: flag = false
flush #4: flag = false
flush #5: flag = false

Let’s drop it and try to flush again:

if !flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
 drop(g1);
 println!("-- T1 unpins --");

 while !flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) && flushes < 10 {
 t2.pin().flush();
 flushes += 1;
 println!("flush #{}: flag = {}", flushes, flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst));
 }
}

We see that the drop doesn’t happen on the first flush, even though nobody is pinned. The reason for this is the rule from Turon’s post: a bag sealed at epoch e may only be freed once the global epoch has reached e + 2. Each flush advances the epoch by at most one step, so it takes two flushes.

-- T1 unpins --
flush #6: flag = false
flush #7: flag = true

Experiment #2: No Pinned Threads

We can try the same experiment but without T1 holding a guard, to verify that it was indeed that guard that was keeping the epoch from advancing, and, in turn, keeping the node from getting dropped.

flush #1: flag = false
flush #2: flag = true

We see that the first flush doesn’t yet trigger a drop(). Instead, what happens with that first flush, is that the “sealed bag” is passed to the global queue, for it to be dropped the next time the epoch advances.

Visualization

Conclusion

Regarding the first part of this post, I wrote it and was very happy with how it turned out, mainly because I found the idea of reclaiming those “unused” bits so simple yet so elegant. It just made my brain happy.

As for the second part, however, I went through many attempts. I didn’t want to just repeat explanations that already exist, but I wanted to give enough context to make the concepts in my experiments clear. I also went back and forth between different experiment ideas. I then realized I had at some point lost my plot and was overcomplicating things. So, I opted for a simpler demonstration that shows the concept of EBR in practice and how it relates to our original problem of a lock-free stack.

The reason I like writing these posts is to test my understanding of a topic by trying to explain it cohesively, and demonstrating it through code. This makes the concept feel more real to me and helps me make sure I got it. I also love and need lots of diagrams, which might also be useful for someone else.

This one in particular wasn’t so straightforward to write, but it was extremely rewarding! I also enjoyed the feedback I’ve gotten from the community along the way. Some of the chats I’ve had made me feel like a scientist in the 20th century, writing letters back and forth to each other, discussing their findings. This is the sense of community I strive for, so I consider this all worth the effort!

As some already know, I’m currently unemployed, so finding meaning and community through what I’m doing means so much to me. Thank you so much for reading and I hope you enjoyed it as well!

  • Keir Fraser, Practical lock-freedom (PhD thesis, University of Cambridge, 2004): where EBR was introduced.
  • Aaron Turon, Lock-freedom without garbage collection: the clearest walkthrough of the algorithm, and the origin of crossbeam-epoch. Check it out for a lock-free stack implementation using crossbeam-epoch to conclude the stack journey.

Using crossbeam-epoch

  • Crossbeam source code

Lock-free linked lists

  • Timothy Harris, A Pragmatic Implementation of Non-Blocking Linked-Lists (DISC 2001).

title: The list of AI insiders sounding the alarm on their own companies keeps growing
description:
Last week, OpenAI safety leader David Robinson resigned from the company, becoming the latest to join what is, in his words, a “parade of former colleagues” who have left roles at AI companies amid concerns about the tech or its use. In a subsequent essay for The Atlantic, he said the “trial and error” approach favored by AI companies must end.

Robinson is far from alone. Here’s a list of other AI researchers and employees who’ve made public warnings about their former employers.

ED NEWTON-REX

In November 2023, Ed Newton-Rex left his role leading the audio team at Stability AI, the maker of text-to-image tool Stable Diffusion, over concerns about the way copyrighted material was being used to train the tech.

“My opinion here doesn’t align with the generative AI industry’s current way of doing things,” Newton-Rex told Fast Company following his resignation, adding that he thought the industry’s prevailing outlook, paired with rapidly advancing tech, would be “very, very bad for creators.” 

Since then, he’s founded Fairly Trained, a nonprofit that issues certifications for AI companies whose data use meets certain requirements.

THE GROUP LETTER

On June 4, 2024, 13 current and former employees of top AI companies published a letter titled “A Right to Warn about Advanced Artificial Intelligence.” In it, they asserted that the technology poses risks ranging from “the further entrenchment of existing inequalities, to manipulation and misinformation, to the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction,” and expressed concerns about a lack of oversight. 

Signatories included former Google DeepMind employee Ramana Kumar, former Anthropic and current Google DeepMind employee Neel Nanda, who leads the company’s mechanistic interpretability team; and 11 current and former OpenAI employees, including Jacob Hilton, who now works for the Alignment Research Center; Daniel Kokotajlo, who founded and leads the nonprofit research group AI Futures Project; William Saunders, Carroll Wainwright, and Daniel Ziegler, the latter of whom now works for Anthropic; and six people who remained anonymous.

Prominent computer scientists Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, and “Godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton also endorsed the letter.

JAN LEIKE

In May 2024, OpenAI Superalignment team lead Jan Leike announced his departure on X, stating that “safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.” Leike, who has also worked at Google’s DeepMind, now heads Anthropic’s alignment team.

“Now is a good time to build institutional mechanisms to pace the frontier of AI development,” he said on X in September. “The industry is locked into an all-out scaling race to build superintelligence as quickly as possible, and we may need to give everyone more time for safety and alignment mitigations.” 

Leike added, “I’m not the only one who believes this,” linking to a statement titled “Pacing the Frontier” signed by 1,386 employees of major AI companies.

SUCHIR BALAJI

After graduating from the University of California, Berkeley, Suchir Balaji was hired by OpenAI, where he spent about four years working on ChatGPT and other projects.

He left the company in August 2024, on the same day as cofounder John Schulman, who said the timing was coincidental. Balaji blew the whistle on what he said were copyright infringements by Open AI, and published an essay online explaining how he thought ChatGPT’s outputs violated Fair Use law. 

That November, he was named as a potential witness in The New York Times’s lawsuit against OpenAI alleging willful copyright infringement.

The 26-year-old was found dead in his San Francisco apartment eight days later. His death was ruled a suicide, though his parents and others raised questions about that determination, as reported by The Guardian.

MRINANK SHARMA 

In February, Mrinank Sharma announced his departure from Anthropic, where he led the Safeguards Research team. 

“I continuously find myself reckoning with our situation,” Sharma wrote in his resignation letter, which he shared on X. “The world is in peril,” he continued, not just from AI and bioweapons, but “a whole series of interconnected crises.”

ALEX TURNER

Alex Turner left his job as a Google DeepMind research scientist in June, after a failed campaign to stop the company from signing a contract that allows the U.S. Pentagon to use its AI “for any lawful government purpose,” which he and others worry may allow for mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. 

Last month, he testified for a U.S. Senate hearing on rogue AI. “Often we think about the movements of our overseas adversaries, but now we must consider how we may be building adversaries at home by training misaligned AI systems,” he said in his written statement.

JACOB COXON

Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from the latter last month. 

“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he said in a viral X post. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

He went on to assert that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

In an interview with PBS in September, Coxon said an AI race with China “could be very bad, and that we should be taking pretty rapid actions for international coordination,” but that he believes the company leaders echoing that desire “are privately quite skeptical” of being able to achieve that cooperation.

MIKITA BALESNI, TOMEK KORBAK, AND JASMINE WANG

Last week, three OpenAI safety and alignment researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive misinformation, which one of them, Tomek Korbak, said online was due to how he’d communicated information to METR, the AI research nonprofit investigating OpenAI’s recent Hugging Face hacking incident.

“AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” the researchers said in the letter they sent to company leadership, which they published online on October 8. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.”

OpenAI released a statement the following day saying the researchers were fired after an internal investigation “found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information,” adding, “We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out.”
